preview_text: The color, discharge, and edge of a wound tell a TCM practitioner whether the healing is stalled by lack of resources, trapped heat, or stagnant blood - and most chronic wounds beg...
categories: ["การบาดเจ็บ แผลไหม้ และบาดแผล"]
synonyms: ["Wound Healing", "Chronic wound healing impairment", "Poor wound healing", "Slow-healing wounds", "Wound Healing Difficulties", "Chronic non-healing wound"]
conventional_description:
In Western medicine, slow wound healing is often a complication of underlying conditions like diabetes, poor circulation, infection, or nutritional deficiencies. A wound that fails to close within the expected timeframe - typically a few weeks - is considered chronic. Diagnosis involves assessing the wound's size, depth, and appearance, along with blood tests to check for infection, blood sugar levels, and nutritional status.
Standard care focuses on keeping the wound clean, removing dead tissue (debridement), applying dressings that maintain a moist environment, and treating any underlying disease. Despite these measures, many chronic wounds persist, leading to frustration and a prolonged recovery.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment for slow-healing wounds includes regular cleaning and debridement, specialized dressings (hydrocolloids, alginates, foams), and sometimes topical antibiotics or antiseptics. If infection is present, oral or intravenous antibiotics are used. For wounds caused by poor circulation, compression therapy or vascular surgery may be recommended. Addressing root causes like high blood sugar in diabetes or malnutrition with supplements is also a key part of care.
tcm_understanding:
TCM views a wound as a local sign of a body-wide imbalance. The skin and muscles are governed by the Spleen and Lungs, while the smooth flow of Qi and Blood through the channels nourishes every tissue. When a wound fails to close, it means the resources to build new flesh - Qi and Blood - are either insufficient, blocked, or being consumed by an ongoing battle with pathogens like Heat and Dampness.
Two broad categories emerge: deficiency and excess. In deficiency patterns, the body simply lacks the raw materials to repair itself. Qi and Blood Deficiency leaves the wound pale and weak, with poor granulation, while Spleen Qi Deficiency adds digestive weakness and fatigue.
In excess patterns, a pathogen is interfering. Toxic-Heat creates a red, hot, pus-filled wound that burns through tissue faster than it can heal. Damp-Heat causes persistent oozing and swelling, while Blood Stagnation starves the wound bed by blocking circulation - the edges turn dark and hard.
Even a less common pattern like Yin Deficiency with Empty-Heat can stall healing, leaving a shallow, dry ulcer that smolders with a low-grade heat. Because each pattern arises from a different organ system and mechanism, the same slow-healing wound can demand entirely different herbs and acupuncture points depending on its root cause. This is why TCM examines not just the wound but the whole person: tongue, pulse, digestion, and energy levels all reveal the true diagnosis.
classical_quote: 「疮口不敛，多由气血两虚，宜服生肌散。」
classical_translation: "When a sore fails to close, it is usually because Qi and Blood are both deficient; one should administer Sheng Ji San."
classical_source:
Wai Ke Zheng Zong (Orthodox Manual of External Medicine)  ,  Chapter on Sores and Ulcers 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by examining the wound itself - its color, discharge, edges, and pain quality. These local signs, together with the person’s overall energy, digestion, and sleep, point toward the underlying pattern that is stalling healing. Tongue appearance and pulse quality provide confirmation, revealing whether the root is a deficiency of vital resources or an excess of heat, dampness, or stagnation.
If the wound looks pale, with thin watery discharge and weak granulation, the root is often Qi and Blood Deficiency. The person feels fatigued and looks pale, with a weak, thready pulse and a pale tongue. When poor appetite, bloating, and loose stools are also present, the deeper cause is Spleen Qi Deficiency - the digestive system fails to transform food into enough Qi and Blood to supply the wound.
When the wound is red, swollen, and oozes thick yellow pus, Toxic-Heat is the main pattern; a red tongue with a yellow coat and a rapid, slippery pulse confirm it.
If the discharge is stickier and the surrounding skin is weepy with a greasy yellow tongue coating, Damp-Heat is trapping moisture and heat, stopping the wound from drying and closing. These two heat patterns often overlap but can be teased apart by the texture of the discharge and tongue coating.
A wound with dark, purplish, hard edges and fixed stabbing pain signals Blood Stagnation, often with a purplish tongue and a choppy pulse. A shallow, dry ulcer that burns and produces little pus, with a red peeled tongue and a thin rapid pulse, points to Empty-Heat from Yin Deficiency - the body’s cooling, moistening resources are depleted, leaving a smoldering inflammation that dries out the wound bed and resists closure.

patterns.symptoms: ["Pale wound bed with weak, slow-growing granulation tissue", "Scanty, clear or watery discharge rather than thick pus", "Surrounding skin looks pale or sallow, not red or swollen", "Fatigue and low energy", "Dizziness or lightheadedness", "Pale or sallow complexion"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and exhaustion, Irregular or poor eating habits, Exposure to cold or drafts, Worry and mental strain
patterns.better_with: Rest and adequate sleep, Warm, nourishing soups and stews, Gentle movement like walking, Keeping the wound covered and warm
patterns.why_this_happens: Qi is the force that drives the body to build new tissue, and Blood is the substance that moistens and nourishes the wound bed. When both are deficient, the body simply lacks the raw materials and energy to close the wound. Granulation tissue grows slowly, appears pale and weak, and the edges fail to pull together, leaving a chronic, indolent sore that shows no signs of infection but refuses to heal.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, may be thin or show teeth marks, with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak, lacking force, especially at the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood are built from rest and nutrient-rich food, and they are consumed by overwork, stress, and cold. When the body is depleted, it cannot spare the resources to close a wound. Rest and warm, nourishing meals replenish the Spleen and generate new Qi and Blood, directly supplying the wound with the materials it needs to fill in and seal over.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize warm, easily digested, nourishing foods such as bone broths, congees with astragalus (Huang Qi) and angelica (Dang Gui), and lightly cooked leafy greens. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that weaken the Spleen. Rest is crucial; protect the wound from cold and drafts, but gentle daily movement like walking helps circulate Qi and Blood to the area without depleting reserves.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen transforms food into Qi and Blood, the raw materials for tissue repair. When Spleen Qi is weak, this transformation is sluggish, so the body lacks the energy and nourishment to generate new flesh. The wound bed looks pale and flaccid, granulation is slow, and closure stalls. The digestive symptoms-poor appetite, bloating, loose stools-are the same deficiency showing up in the gut.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy body with tooth marks, thin white coating. Pulse: weak and soft, especially at the right Guan (middle) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen transforms food into Qi and Blood, the building blocks for wound healing. Cold and raw foods directly damage Spleen Yang, slowing digestion and reducing the energy available for tissue repair. Excessive worry knots the Spleen Qi, further impairing its ability to generate new flesh.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, easily digestible foods such as congee, soups, and steamed vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that tax the Spleen. Eat at regular intervals and in moderate amounts. Get adequate rest and avoid overworking, as the Spleen thrives on routine and calm.

patterns.symptoms: ["Wound oozes sticky, yellowish fluid", "Wound edges are red and swollen", "Feeling of heaviness and sluggishness in the body", "Sticky or greasy sensation in the mouth", "Poor appetite and loose, sticky stools"]
patterns.worse_with: Hot, humid weather, Greasy, fried, or sweet foods, Alcohol and coffee, Prolonged sitting or inactivity
patterns.better_with: Dry, well-ventilated environment, Light, bland meals, Frequent dressing changes
patterns.why_this_happens: Dampness and Heat are two pathological factors that easily combine and get trapped in the tissues. In a wound, Dampness creates swelling and persistent oozing-a sticky, heavy fluid that keeps the area wet and prevents the wound edges from coming together. The Heat component fuels low-grade inflammation, causing redness, warmth, and a yellowish discharge. Together they form a boggy, inflamed environment where new skin and flesh cannot grow, so the wound stays open and slow to heal.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a thick, yellow, greasy coating. Pulse: soggy-rapid (Ru Shu) or slippery-rapid (Hua Shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat feeds on moisture and richness. Humid weather and heavy, greasy foods add to the internal Dampness and Heat, making the wound wetter and more inflamed. Keeping the environment dry and eating light, bland foods drains Dampness and cools Heat, creating the opposite conditions. Changing dressings prevents the local accumulation of Dampness, while gentle movement keeps Qi and fluids moving so they don't stagnate around the wound.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, and sweet foods, as well as dairy and alcohol-these all generate Dampness and feed Heat. Favor light, bland, easily digestible foods like barley, mung beans, cucumber, and bitter greens. Keep the wound clean and dry, and change dressings frequently to prevent fluid from pooling. Gentle movement helps Qi circulate, but avoid humid, sweaty environments that add external Dampness.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed stabbing pain at the wound site", "Dark purplish or dusky wound edges", "Pain worse at night and with pressure", "Hard, lumpy tissue around the wound", "Dark or purplish tongue with stasis spots"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold exposure or cold drinks, Prolonged sitting or inactivity, Emotional stress and frustration, Heavy, greasy, or cold foods, Pressure on the wound
patterns.better_with: Warm compresses on the area, Gentle movement and stretching, Eating warming blood-moving foods (turmeric, garlic), Keeping the wound clean and covered, Relaxation and stress relief
patterns.why_this_happens:
When blood flow becomes stagnant, fresh oxygen and nutrients cannot reach the wound bed, and metabolic waste builds up locally. This starves the tissue of the resources it needs to build new skin, so the wound stalls and refuses to close.
The edges of the wound turn dark or purplish and feel hard to the touch, because the stuck blood creates a kind of internal “traffic jam.” The pain is fixed and stabbing, often worse at night and with pressure, which reflects the blocked circulation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dusky body with stasis spots, engorged dark sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩 sè) and rough, or wiry (弦 xián).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and inactivity cause blood to congeal and stagnate further, blocking the delivery of healing nutrients. Warmth and gentle movement encourage blood to flow smoothly, bringing fresh oxygen and immune cells to the wound. Emotional stress tightens the Liver Qi, which in turn constricts blood vessels and worsens stasis, so relaxation helps the wound heal.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the wound area warm but not hot. Gentle daily movement like walking helps blood circulate. Include warming spices such as turmeric, ginger, and black pepper in meals. Avoid cold, raw foods and iced drinks that congeal blood. Emotional balance is important-stress tightens circulation.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Toxic-Heat invades a wound, it creates intense inflammation that continuously damages newly forming tissue. The redness, swelling, and thick yellow pus are signs that the body is fighting a deep, hot infection. This ongoing battle consumes Qi and Blood, preventing the wound from closing and leaving it stuck in a destructive cycle of pus formation and tissue breakdown.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with prickly thorns and a dry yellow coating. Pulse: rapid, forceful, and often slippery.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Toxic-Heat is a combination of intense Heat and infective Toxin. Spicy, greasy foods and alcohol add more Heat to the body, while stress stirs up internal Fire. A hot environment can further inflame the wound. Cooling foods and clean, cool wound care help drain the Heat, while rest conserves Qi so the body can fight the infection and begin to close the wound.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol, which all add Heat. Eat cooling, light foods like mung beans, cucumber, and watermelon. Keep the wound clean and dry, and use a cool, damp cloth to gently clean the area. Rest to conserve energy for healing.

patterns.worse_with: Late nights and overwork, Spicy, fried, or drying foods, Worry and mental strain, Dry, heated indoor air
patterns.better_with: Cool, humid environment, Rest and adequate sleep, Moisturizing the wound, Pear and lily bulb soup
patterns.why_this_happens: Yin is the body's cooling and moistening foundation. When it runs low, a subtle, smoldering heat ignites-like a kettle boiling dry. This empty heat rises and dries out the wound bed, leaving the skin parched and unable to form healthy new tissue. The result is a shallow, stubborn ulcer that looks dry, feels tender, and refuses to close, often worsening at night when the body's natural Yin should be deepest.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, and dry with little or no coating, often with cracks. Pulse: fine (thready) and rapid, especially weak at the rear position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin is the body's coolant and moisture reserve. Late nights, stress, and spicy food consume Yin and fan the flames of empty heat, which dries the wound further. Rest, cooling foods, and a moist environment help rebuild Yin and settle the heat, giving the tissue the fluid nourishment it needs to finally close.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize deep, restorative sleep-this is when Yin rebuilds. Eat moistening, cooling foods like pear, lily bulb, black sesame, and tofu. Avoid alcohol, coffee, and spicy or fried foods that stoke internal heat. Gentle, calming activities like tai chi or slow walking are better than intense, sweat-inducing exercise.

faqs.question: Can TCM help if my wound has been open for months?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially if conventional care has stalled. TCM looks for the internal reason the wound isn't closing - like poor digestion failing to make enough Qi and Blood, or hidden Damp-Heat keeping the wound wet. By treating the underlying pattern, many chronic wounds that have plateaued begin to show new granulation within a few weeks.

faqs.question: Do I still need to use my prescribed wound dressings?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. TCM internal treatment works alongside good wound care. Keep the wound clean, change dressings as directed, and follow your doctor's debridement schedule. Herbs and acupuncture are not a substitute for proper topical care but can accelerate healing when used together.

faqs.question: What does acupuncture do for a wound that's already open?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture points are chosen on the body, not directly in the wound. Points like Zusanli ST-36 and Sanyinjiao SP-6 strengthen the Spleen and build Qi and Blood. Local points near the wound (but not in it) can improve circulation to the area. The goal is to send the body's healing resources to the wound site and correct the internal imbalance.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Often yes, because the Spleen's ability to extract Qi from food directly affects wound healing. A TCM practitioner may recommend warm, cooked foods and avoiding cold, raw, or greasy items that weaken digestion. In Damp-Heat patterns, reducing damp-producing foods like dairy and sugar is especially important.

faqs.question: Is it safe to take Chinese herbs with my diabetes or blood pressure medications?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, but you must inform both your prescribing doctor and your TCM practitioner about all medications and supplements. Some Blood-moving herbs (like Dang Gui or Chuan Xiong) may interact with anticoagulants. A qualified TCM practitioner will choose formulas that are safe alongside your existing medications.

faqs.question: How do I know which pattern I have?
faqs.answer: Look at the wound and your overall symptoms. A pale, weak wound with fatigue suggests deficiency; a red, hot, pus-filled wound suggests Toxic-Heat; a dark, hard-edged wound with stabbing pain suggests Blood Stagnation. However, many cases involve mixed patterns, so a professional tongue and pulse diagnosis is the most reliable way to get the right treatment.
